purpose: 60 additional original, one-fact AQA school-mock core flashcards, with explicit valid paraphrase and wrong misconception for real website marker.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why does percentage uncertainty in wire diameter approximately double for cross-sectional area?
records.originalBack: Area A = πd²/4, so percentage uncertainty in A ≈ 2 × percentage uncertainty in d.
accept: Area varies as diameter squared, so the percentage area uncertainty is twice the percentage diameter uncertainty.
reject: The percentage uncertainty in area is half the percentage uncertainty in wire diameter.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why does increasing the measured interval often reduce percentage uncertainty?
records.originalBack: The absolute uncertainty is similar but becomes a smaller fraction of a larger measured value.
accept: A larger measured interval has a smaller relative uncertainty for the same absolute reading error.
reject: Percentage uncertainty increases automatically whenever the measured interval increases.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A 12 N force is 30° from the vertical. Find its horizontal and vertical components.
records.originalBack: Horizontal = 12 sin30° = 6.0 N; vertical = 12 cos30° ≈ 10.4 N.
accept: Horizontal 6.0 N and vertical approximately 10.4 N.
reject: Horizontal 10.4 N and vertical 6.0 N.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does crossing the time axis on a velocity–time graph mean?
records.originalBack: Velocity passes through zero and changes sign: the object stops momentarily, then reverses direction.
accept: A sign change in velocity means the object is briefly at rest then travels in the opposite direction.
reject: Crossing zero velocity proves that acceleration is zero at that instant.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A displacement–time curve has a positive gradient which becomes less steep. What happens to velocity?
records.originalBack: Velocity remains positive but decreases: the object moves forwards while slowing down.
accept: Its gradient stays positive but falls, so velocity is positive and decreasing.
reject: A less steep positive displacement-time gradient means negative velocity.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does a horizontal velocity–time graph below the time axis show?
records.originalBack: Constant negative velocity; acceleration is zero. The object is moving, not stationary.
accept: The object moves with an unchanging velocity in the negative direction and zero acceleration.
reject: A flat velocity-time line below zero indicates zero velocity and no motion.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How does the normal reaction change on an incline without other perpendicular forces?
records.originalBack: R = mg cos θ.
accept: On an incline of angle theta with no other perpendicular components, the contact force is mg cos theta.
reject: The normal reaction on a slope always equals mg sin theta.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the weight component down a slope of angle θ?
records.originalBack: mg sin θ.
accept: Down-slope component of weight is mg sin(theta).
reject: The weight component parallel to the slope is mg cos theta.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A 20 N force acts at 30° to a 0.50 m lever arm. Find its moment about the pivot.
records.originalBack: M = Fr sinθ = 20×0.50×sin30° = 5.0 N m.
accept: 5.0 newton metres, from 20 times 0.50 times sin 30 degrees.
reject: 10.0 N m, because the sine factor can be omitted.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the principle of moments in equilibrium?
records.originalBack: Total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment about the same point.
accept: For rotational equilibrium the sum of moments clockwise equals the sum anticlockwise about one pivot.
reject: For equilibrium clockwise moments must exceed anticlockwise moments.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What condition allows use of conservation of momentum?
records.originalBack: No external resultant force acts on the system.
accept: Momentum of a system is conserved if the net external force on that system is zero.
reject: Momentum is conserved only when every object has zero velocity.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Give three electrical power equations.
records.originalBack: P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
accept: Power equals voltage times current, current squared times resistance, or voltage squared divided by resistance.
reject: P=V/I=IR=V/R for an electrical component.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the ultimate tensile stress?
records.originalBack: Maximum tensile stress before breaking.
accept: Ultimate tensile stress is the greatest stress attained in a tensile test.
reject: Ultimate tensile stress is the strain at which a material first begins to deform.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is tensile strain?
records.originalBack: strain = ΔL/L; it has no unit.
accept: The extension divided by original length, with no dimensions.
reject: Strain equals applied force divided by cross-sectional area in pascals.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is wavelength?
records.originalBack: Shortest distance between two points in phase.
accept: Wavelength is the shortest separation of two positions vibrating in phase on a progressive wave.
reject: Wavelength is the distance travelled by a wave in half a period.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: For a string fixed at both ends, what is the first-harmonic wavelength?
records.originalBack: Twice the vibrating length, λ = 2L.
accept: The first harmonic on a string fixed at both ends has wavelength 2 times the length.
reject: For a string with fixed ends the fundamental wavelength equals the string length.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What happens to fringe spacing if the double-slit separation increases?
records.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: Larger slit spacing means smaller fringe spacing, with all else unchanged.
reject: Increasing double-slit separation increases fringe spacing.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What happens to fringe spacing if the screen distance increases?
records.originalBack: It increases.
accept: Fringe spacing scales directly with the distance from slits to screen.
reject: Moving the screen farther from the slits makes fringe spacing smaller.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the critical-angle equation for air outside a material?
records.originalBack: sin c = 1/n.
accept: For a material surrounded by air, the critical angle obeys sin c=1/n.
reject: At an air interface the critical-angle rule is sin c=n.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does the gradient of resistance against wire length give?
records.originalBack: ρ/A, for a wire of constant cross-section.
accept: The R against L slope equals resistivity divided by cross-sectional area.
reject: The resistance-length gradient is the resistivity times cross-sectional area.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How many electrons are in a 3+ ion formed from Z=13?
records.originalBack: 13−3 = 10 electrons; the nucleus is unchanged.
accept: An aluminium ion with charge 3+ and Z=13 contains ten electrons.
reject: A 3+ ion with proton number 13 has 16 electrons.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the purpose of ionisation in TOF?
records.originalBack: To give sample particles an electrical charge so they can be accelerated and detected.
accept: TOF ionisation makes charged ions that electric fields can accelerate and a detector can register.
reject: Ionisation in TOF gives every atom the same mass and removes isotope differences.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Write the second ionisation equation for magnesium.
records.originalBack: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻.
accept: Mg+(g) to Mg2+(g) plus an electron.
reject: Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e- is the second ionisation equation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How many electrons can an s, p and d subshell hold?
accept: The subshell electron capacities are s 2, p 6, d 10.
reject: The electron capacities of s, p and d are 2, 8 and 18.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the difference between empirical and molecular formula?
records.originalBack: Empirical: simplest atom ratio. Molecular: actual atoms per molecule.
accept: Empirical gives the lowest whole-number atom ratio; molecular gives actual atoms in one molecule.
reject: An empirical formula always has more atoms than the molecular formula.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What are the three stages of empirical formula calculation?
records.originalBack: Divide element masses by Ar; divide moles by smallest; find integer ratio.
accept: Convert each mass to moles, divide by the least, then scale to whole numbers.
reject: To find empirical formula, divide each mass by the largest atomic number and stop.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How is molecular formula calculated from empirical formula?
records.originalBack: Find empirical-formula Mr, divide molecular Mr by it, multiply subscripts.
accept: Divide measured molecular Mr by empirical-formula mass, then multiply empirical subscripts by that integer.
reject: Molecular formula is found by dividing each empirical subscript by the molecular Mr.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How do you calculate molar mass of an unknown gas from mass and gas data?
records.originalBack: First n=pV/(RT), then molar mass M=m/n.
accept: Obtain moles from pV= nRT and divide measured gas mass by n.
reject: The molar mass of a gas equals its pressure divided by its volume.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define a single covalent bond accurately.
records.originalBack: One electron pair shared between atoms and attracted to both nuclei.
accept: A covalent bond is the attraction of two nuclei for one shared pair of electrons.
reject: A single covalent bond is attraction between two oppositely charged ions.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is a coordinate or dative covalent bond?
records.originalBack: A shared pair where both electrons originate from one atom.
accept: Both electrons in a dative shared pair are supplied by one donor atom.
reject: A coordinate bond forms when each atom supplies one electron to the pair.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How many covalent bonds does each carbon make in diamond?
records.originalBack: Four, in a three-dimensional tetrahedral network.
accept: In diamond every carbon makes four strong covalent bonds in a tetrahedral network.
reject: In diamond every carbon atom forms three bonds and has one delocalised electron.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
records.originalBack: No mobile ions or delocalised electrons are available.
accept: Diamond has no mobile charge carriers, because its valence electrons are localised in bonds.
reject: Diamond conducts because each carbon has a mobile delocalised electron.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define enthalpy of hydration.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions becomes hydrated, forming aqueous ions.
accept: Hydration enthalpy is the change when one mole of gaseous ions becomes aqueous ions.
reject: Hydration enthalpy is the change for aqueous ions becoming isolated gaseous ions.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define lattice enthalpy of formation.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a solid ionic compound is formed from its constituent gaseous ions.
accept: One mole of solid ionic lattice is formed from its separate gaseous ions.
reject: Lattice formation enthalpy is the change on splitting a solid into gaseous ions.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define enthalpy of solution.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of solute dissolves in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution.
accept: One mole of solute dissolves in sufficient solvent for effectively infinite dilution.
reject: Enthalpy of solution means forming a solid from its free gaseous ions.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define standard enthalpy of formation.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
accept: One mole of compound is made from its elements in standard states under standard conditions.
reject: Standard enthalpy of formation is defined for forming two moles of compound from gaseous atoms.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: State Hess's law.
records.originalBack: Overall enthalpy change is independent of pathway if start/end states match.
accept: The same reactants and products have the same enthalpy difference irrespective of reaction pathway.
reject: Hess's law says activation energy is independent of the route taken.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the combustion-enthalpy Hess calculation?
records.originalBack: Sum combustion enthalpies of reactants minus those of products.
accept: Use the total combustion enthalpy of reactants minus that of products, accounting for coefficients.
reject: For combustion enthalpy cycles always subtract reactants from products.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why do equation coefficients matter in Hess calculations?
records.originalBack: Multiply each substance's molar enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient.
accept: Enthalpies in a Hess cycle are multiplied by the balanced equation's coefficients.
reject: Hess enthalpy totals should ignore coefficients in the equation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the trend in Group 2 hydroxide solubility?
records.originalBack: Solubility increases down the group.
accept: Group 2 metal hydroxides generally dissolve more readily as you go down the group.
reject: Group 2 hydroxides become less soluble going from magnesium to barium.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Write the net ionic equation for barium sulfate precipitation.
records.originalBack: Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s).
accept: Ba2+(aq) plus SO4 2-(aq) produces BaSO4(s).
reject: Ba2+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> BaCl(s) is the sulfate precipitation equation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What does the overall order of a rate equation mean?
records.originalBack: It is the sum of the powers of all concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate equation.
accept: Overall reaction order is obtained by adding the exponents of the concentration terms.
reject: Overall order is the number of compounds appearing in a balanced chemical equation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How do you calculate Ea from the gradient of ln k against 1/T?
records.originalBack: Ea = −gradient × R. Convert J mol⁻¹ to kJ mol⁻¹ at the end if required.
accept: Multiply the negative slope of ln k against inverse kelvin temperature by the gas constant R.
reject: Activation energy equals the Arrhenius graph gradient divided by R.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What goes into a Kp expression?
records.originalBack: Partial pressures of gaseous equilibrium species, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.
accept: Use equilibrium partial pressures, products over reactants, with the powers given by stoichiometric coefficients.
reject: Use only the concentrations of solids in a Kp expression.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Define second electron affinity.
records.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous 1− ions each gains an electron, forming gaseous 2− ions.
accept: The change for one mole of gaseous singly negative ions each gaining another electron to form 2- ions.
reject: Second electron affinity is removal of one mole of electrons from gaseous 1- ions.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why does negative ΔG not guarantee a rapid reaction?
records.originalBack: ΔG predicts thermodynamic feasibility, not rate. A high activation energy can make the reaction very slow.
accept: A spontaneous-feasible reaction may still proceed slowly when activation energy is high.
reject: Negative Gibbs free-energy change guarantees an instantaneous reaction.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.section: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
records.front: At 25 °C, what is Kw?
records.originalBack: 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶.
accept: At 298 K, Kw is 1.0 x 10^-14 mol^2 dm^-6.
reject: At 25 degrees Celsius Kw is 1.0 x 10^-7 mol^2 dm^-6.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What causes optical isomerism?
records.originalBack: A chiral carbon bonded to four different groups gives non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers.
accept: A stereogenic carbon with four different groups can generate nonsuperimposable mirror-image structures.
reject: Optical isomerism occurs whenever a carbon atom has two identical substituents.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why can distilled water be added to the conical flask during a titration?
records.originalBack: It changes concentration but not the number of moles being titrated.
accept: Water added to the conical flask does not change the number of analyte moles already transferred.
reject: Adding distilled water into the titration flask creates extra moles of analyte.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the range of a function?
records.originalBack: Its possible output values.
accept: Range refers to the collection of outputs a function can take.
reject: The range of a function is its allowed input values.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the domain of f(x) = √x over the real numbers?
accept: x must be greater than or equal to zero for real square root x.
reject: The real domain of square root x is all negative real numbers.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x−2)?
records.originalBack: All real x except x = 2.
accept: All real numbers other than 2, where the denominator vanishes.
reject: x=2 is included in the domain of 1/(x-2).

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How are gradients of two nonvertical perpendicular lines related?
records.originalBack: Their gradients multiply to −1.
accept: For two nonvertical perpendicular lines, m1*m2=-1.
reject: Two nonvertical perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is +1.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the gradient between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂)?
records.originalBack: m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁).
accept: Change in y divided by change in x: (y2-y1)/(x2-x1).
reject: Gradient equals (x2-x1)/(y2-y1) in general.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is true of the gradients of two non-vertical parallel lines?
records.originalBack: They are equal.
accept: Parallel nonvertical straight lines have the same slope.
reject: Parallel straight lines always have gradient product -1.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: At which angles in degrees is tan θ undefined?
records.originalBack: 90° + 180°n, for any integer n.
accept: 90 degrees plus an integer multiple of 180 degrees.
reject: tan theta is undefined at all multiples of 180 degrees.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is logₐ1?
records.originalBack: 0, since a⁰ = 1 (a > 0, a ≠ 1).
accept: The logarithm to any valid base of 1 is 0.
reject: log_a(1)=1 for a>0 and a not equal to 1.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is logₐa?
records.originalBack: 1, for a > 0 and a ≠ 1.
accept: The logarithm of its own valid base equals one.
reject: log_a(a)=0 for any valid base a.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: State the logarithm quotient law for logₐ(x/y).
records.originalBack: logₐ(x/y) = logₐx − logₐy (x,y>0; a>0, a≠1).
accept: The log of a quotient is the log of numerator minus the log of denominator.
reject: log_a(x/y)=log_a(x)+log_a(y).

records.subject: Maths
records.front: Why is +C needed in an indefinite integral?
records.originalBack: Differentiation removes constant terms, so every constant shift is an antiderivative.
accept: All antiderivatives differ by an arbitrary additive constant that disappears on differentiation.
reject: An indefinite integral has no arbitrary constant because differentiation preserves constants.
